data.title: Analog Devices Bets $1.35 Billion on Edge AI with Alif Semiconductor Deal
data.description:
Analog Devices (NASDAQ: ADI) has agreed to acquire Alif Semiconductor for $1.35 billion in cash, adding low-power edge-AI processors to a portfolio built around sensing, signal processing and power management. The deal gives ADI a larger position in AI that runs inside physical devices rather than only in large data centers.

In its September 9 announcement, Analog Devices said the transaction also includes up to $200 million of contingent consideration. The boards of both companies approved the agreement. ADI expects the deal to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to customary conditions and the expiration of the applicable U.S. antitrust waiting period.

Alif makes microcontrollers and fusion processors with integrated AI and machine-learning acceleration. The company says its architecture combines neural processing with connectivity, security and power management. ADI said Alif's silicon is already shipping in production and has design wins among consumer and industrial customers. Those details support the strategic rationale, but they do not establish the target's revenue or the eventual return on ADI's investment.

The acquisition extends ADI's existing strengths at the boundary between the physical and digital worlds. The company supplies technologies used to sense motion, sound, vibration and other real-world signals, while Alif adds more of the local compute used to interpret those signals. The result could help ADI offer more complete systems for industrial automation, robotics, healthcare, energy and other applications, although the commercial benefits remain management expectations rather than reported results.

That edge focus is the deal's clearest distinction. The Next Web reported that Alif's processors are designed to run neural-network workloads inside devices, limiting the need to send every task to a remote data center. For battery-powered or time-sensitive equipment, local inference can be useful, but the addressable market, customer adoption and competitive response are still developing.

ADI's Form 8-K identifies ADI's Nasdaq ticker and confirms that regulatory clearance is part of the closing process. Investors will therefore have to watch the timetable, the integration of Alif's technology and whether production design wins translate into measurable revenue. The announcement is material for ADI's product strategy, but it does not by itself prove a change in near-term earnings or share-price direction.

data.title: August CPI Preview: Inflation Data Arrives as Oil and Bond Yields Pressure Fed Outlook
data.description:
The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics is scheduled to release August consumer-price data Friday at 8:30 a.m. Eastern, placing a fresh inflation reading just four days before the Federal Reserve's September policy meeting. The report could help determine whether recent pressure from energy markets is beginning to reach households and businesses.

The release is a confirmed event, not yet a confirmed result. The official BLS schedule lists August CPI for September 11 at 8:30 a.m. ET. Investors will be looking at both the monthly change and the year-over-year rate, along with the measure excluding food and energy. The composition matters because a broad pickup would carry a different policy signal from a move concentrated in fuel or other volatile categories.

The timing follows a hotter producer-price report. StockInvest's earlier coverage noted that August producer prices rose 0.4% from July and were up 5.4% from a year earlier, with energy prices accounting for most of the monthly goods increase. Producer prices measure costs earlier in the supply chain, however, so they are not a direct forecast of the consumer result.

Energy markets have made the inflation question more urgent. The Associated Press reported that Brent crude briefly topped $108 a barrel Thursday as the conflict involving Iran disrupted oil flows, while the S&P 500 fell 0.6% and the Nasdaq composite lost 0.7%. Early Friday, AP reported Brent near $105 and U.S. crude around $100 as Asian markets tracked Wall Street's decline. Those moves describe market conditions around the release; they do not establish what August CPI will show.

The Fed's official calendar lists a two-day meeting for September 15–16. A hotter-than-expected CPI reading could reinforce concerns that the central bank has less room to ease policy while energy costs are rising. A softer reading could reduce that pressure, although policymakers would still have to weigh the producer data, employment conditions and the risk that September fuel prices affect later inflation reports.

For stock-market readers, the most important detail may be whether core prices remain contained while headline inflation absorbs the energy shock. That distinction can influence rate-sensitive companies and long-duration technology shares through interest-rate expectations, but the CPI report alone will not determine the Fed's decision or any individual stock's next move.

data.title: What’s Ahead for the Stock Market This Week
data.description:
After Friday’s sharp selloff triggered by President Trump’s decision to raise tariffs in response to China tightening rare earth exports, investors are starting the week on edge. The focus now shifts to trade tensions, earnings season, and the Federal Reserve’s next moves.

Big Earnings Week: Banks and Chipmakers Take Center Stage

This week kicks off a busy stretch of third-quarter results from major financial firms and tech companies.

  • Banks: JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, and Citigroup all report on Tuesday, followed by Bank of America and Morgan Stanley on Wednesday. Later in the week, American Express, Truist Financial, and State Street will wrap up the financial lineup.
  • Tech & Chips: Taiwan Semiconductor (TSMC) reports Thursday after strong AI chip sales boosted its revenue 40% in the first half of 2025. ASML follows on Wednesday after raising concerns about tariffs and slowing demand for chip equipment.
  • Tech events: Oracle’s AI World conference begins Monday, and Salesforce’s Dreamforce starts Tuesday — both likely to bring attention to artificial intelligence and enterprise tech. Earnings Calendar >>

Data Delays and Fed Watch

The federal government shutdown, now entering its third week, is likely to delay several key reports, including retail sales, inflation (PPI), housing starts, and jobless claims. Some data will still come through, like the NFIB Small Business Optimism Index on Tuesday and homebuilder confidence on Thursday.

Investors will also tune in to Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell’s speech on Tuesday, along with comments from Fed officials, including Michelle Bowman and Christopher Waller. The Fed’s Beige Book, which gives an overview of economic conditions across regions, will be released on Wednesday.

Market Context

Bond markets will be closed on Monday for Columbus Day (also observed as Indigenous Peoples Day), but stock exchanges will remain open.

With limited economic data and uncertainty around Washington’s budget standoff, markets are likely to take their cues from corporate earnings and Fed commentary.

In short, this week is about navigating through noise — balancing worries over tariffs and the shutdown against potential optimism from strong bank and chipmaker earnings.

data.title: What Is the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA)? A Complete Guide
data.description:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA), often referred to as the Dow Jones, the Dow 30, or simply the Dow, is one of the world’s most recognized stock market indexes. The DJIA tracks 30 of the largest publicly traded companies in the United States, making it a widely followed indicator of the overall health of the U.S. economy and stock market. Investors searching for DJIA today, DJIA futures, or Dow Jones price updates often turn to this index as a barometer of market sentiment.

But what exactly is the DJIA, what stocks does it include, and how do traders and long-term investors use it in their strategies?

What Is the DJIA?

The Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) is a price-weighted index created in 1896 by Charles Dow and Edward Jones. Unlike market-cap-weighted indexes like the S&P 500, the DJIA assigns weight based on a stock’s price rather than its market capitalization. This means a company with a higher stock price (e.g., Apple or UnitedHealth) influences the index more heavily than lower-priced stocks.

The DJIA is designed to reflect the performance of blue-chip companies across different sectors of the U.S. economy. It does not include utilities or transportation stocks, which are tracked by separate Dow indexes.

What Companies Are in the DJIA?

The DJIA is composed of 30 large, publicly traded U.S. companies that are considered leaders in their industries. These companies span sectors such as technology, finance, healthcare, consumer goods, and industrials.

Here’s a snapshot of the DJIA holdings (as of 2025, September 15th):

How Does the DJIA Work?

  • Price-Weighted Methodology: Higher-priced stocks have more influence.
  • Dow Divisor: A proprietary number adjusted for stock splits, dividends, and corporate actions ensures continuity.
  • Sector Balance: While tech stocks (Apple, Microsoft) now hold significant weight, the index aims to represent the broader U.S. economy.

If Apple (AAPL) rises $5 in a day, it has the same impact on the DJIA as Boeing (BA) rising $5, even though their market caps differ drastically.

Why Do Investors Watch the DJIA?

  • Economic Barometer: The DJIA today is seen as a snapshot of the U.S. economy.
  • Historical Importance: Created in 1896, it has over 125 years of market history.
  • Market Sentiment: Widely quoted on news outlets and financial platforms.
  • Trading Opportunities: Investors follow DJIA futures, DJIA ETFs, and Dow Jones index funds for exposure.

How to Trade or Invest in the DJIA

Investors can’t buy the DJIA directly but can gain exposure through exchange-traded funds (ETFs), futures contracts, or mutual funds:

  • SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (DIA) – tracks the DJIA closely.
  • DJIA Futures – contracts traded on CME, allowing leveraged exposure.

data.title: ECB Raises Deposit Rate to 2.50% as Energy Inflation Persists
data.description:
The European Central Bank raised its three key interest rates by a quarter percentage point on September 10, responding to persistent energy-driven inflation. The decision adds a fresh tightening measure to a market backdrop already strained by higher fuel costs.

Under the ECB decision, the deposit rate will rise to 2.50% on September 16. The main refinancing and marginal lending rates will increase to 2.65% and 2.90%, respectively.

Staff now project headline inflation of 3.0% in 2026, 2.5% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028. The forecasts for the latter two years were raised from June. Growth projections also improved for 2026 and 2027, to 0.9% and 1.4%, reflecting a more resilient economy.

The ECB warned that the outlook carries upside inflation risks and downside growth risks. It did not commit to further rate moves. That leaves the next decision dependent on incoming evidence rather than establishing an automatic series of increases.

The announcement follows another sign of energy pressure in the United States. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that August producer prices rose 0.4% for the month, with final-demand energy prices up 4.2%. StockInvest's earlier coverage examines that release separately.

For stock-market readers, the combination presents two distinct pressures: energy costs can squeeze operating margins, while tighter credit can restrain spending and investment. Those are potential channels, not evidence of a specific share-price reaction. Europe's policy decision also does not determine the Federal Reserve's next move.

data.title: U.S. Producer Inflation Reaches 5.4% as Energy Costs Rebound
data.description:
U.S. producer prices rose 0.4% in August as energy costs rebounded, putting inflation back in focus ahead of next week's Federal Reserve meeting. The September 10 release showed annual producer inflation at 5.4%, up from July's revised 4.8%.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics report showed a 1.1% monthly increase in goods prices. Energy accounted for more than three-quarters of that rise: energy prices increased 4.2%, while diesel jumped 24.1%. Services prices rose a more modest 0.1%.

The picture was less severe after stripping out volatile categories. Prices excluding food, energy and trade services increased 0.3% for the month, following July's 0.4% rise. That measure remained up 4.7% from a year earlier. The divergence points to an energy-led acceleration in the headline figure rather than a uniform pickup across the economy.

For businesses exposed to fuel and freight, the release highlights renewed cost pressure. How much reaches customers depends on companies' ability to raise prices; firms that absorb higher costs could face pressure on margins.

The next inflation checkpoint is the August Consumer Price Index, scheduled for September 11 at 8:30 a.m. Eastern, according to the official BLS calendar. It measures a different stage of pricing, so the producer report should not be read as a direct forecast of the consumer result.

The Fed's September 15–16 meeting will also include updated economic projections. Together, the two inflation releases will give policymakers fresh evidence before that decision, but the PPI result alone does not establish the direction of the next rate move.

data.title: Chewy Raises 2026 Outlook, but Temporary Benefits Lift Quarterly Profit
data.description:
Chewy (NYSE: CHWY) raised its fiscal 2026 outlook on September 9 after quarterly sales increased 7.3%. The online pet retailer's update points to improving profitability, but management cautioned that temporary benefits helped the quarter and its forecast does not assume a meaningful consumer recovery.

In its earnings release, Chewy reported revenue of $3.33 billion for the second quarter ended August 2. Growth was 5.7% excluding contributions from SmartPak and Modern Animal, separating the existing business's expansion from the additional sales those operations brought in.

Net income reached $80.5 million, compared with $62 million a year earlier. GAAP diluted earnings rose to $0.20 per share from $0.14, while adjusted diluted earnings increased to $0.36 from $0.33. Adjusted EBITDA was $226.7 million, with its margin rising to 6.8% from 5.9%. Gross margin held steady at 30.4%.

The earnings-call transcript adds an important qualification. Chief Financial Officer Chris Deppe said about $10 million of upside came from timing benefits, mainly earlier tariff refunds and rebates shifted from the second half. More than $5 million came from discrete items. Together, those factors accounted for essentially all of adjusted EBITDA's outperformance against management's expectations; they should not be treated as a recurring margin improvement.

Chewy now forecasts annual sales of $13.46 billion to $13.57 billion. It also lifted the bottom of its adjusted EBITDA margin range to 6.7% from 6.6%, keeping the upper end at 6.8%. Deppe said the sales midpoint assumes consumer conditions remain broadly consistent with recent months.

The update calls for stronger annual results without a spending rebound. Part of the quarterly upside simply arrived earlier, limiting what it adds to the annual outlook.

data.title: CooperCompanies Cuts 2026 Outlook, Keeps CooperSurgical After Review
data.description:
CooperCompanies (NASDAQ: COO) lowered its fiscal 2026 outlook on September 9 as inventory reductions weighed on its contact lens business. The medical device company also ended a strategic review by deciding to keep CooperSurgical, leaving both operating divisions under the same roof.

The updated forecast calls for annual revenue of $4.229 billion to $4.252 billion and adjusted earnings of $4.51 to $4.55 per share. Its June forecast had projected revenue of $4.285 billion to $4.321 billion and adjusted earnings of $4.58 to $4.66 per share.

For the third quarter ended July 31, revenue rose 1% from a year earlier to $1.066 billion. Adjusted earnings per share increased 4% to $1.15. GAAP earnings reached $2.24 per share, but included a $307.2 million discrete tax benefit; that figure should not be read as a comparable improvement in operating performance.

Chief Executive Al White said reductions in U.S. channel inventory hurt third-quarter results and would continue into the fourth quarter. CooperVision revenue was flat year over year at $717 million.

In a separate announcement, the board said it had considered selling CooperSurgical during the review, which began in December 2025. After evaluating offers, directors unanimously concluded that continued ownership offered shareholders a better outcome than a transaction at this time. The company remains open to future alternatives, so the decision resolves the current review without ruling out a later deal.

The board also increased its total share repurchase authorization from $2 billion to $3 billion. Cooper said it had bought back $445 million of shares during the current fiscal year. The expanded authorization allows further repurchases as part of the company’s revised approach to capital allocation.

Cooper outlined changes to expand CooperVision’s sales and marketing organization and improve inventory management and logistics. CooperSurgical will focus on organic growth and operating improvements. Investing.com’s report also described those priorities, which put the immediate emphasis on improving the existing businesses following the decision against a sale.

data.title: Morgan Stanley Downgrades Daimler Truck Amid Signs of Peak Truck Cycle
data.description:
Morgan Stanley decided to move Daimler Truck Holding AG (DTGGe) from overweight to equal-weight Friday, after the stock surged about 50% from last year's lows. The rating change isn't because the fundamentals suddenly turned sour but rather because the valuation is now pushing the upper limits of what's been seen historically.

Analysts at Morgan Stanley raised the price target slightly to €50 from €47, based on a bumped-up 2027 earnings per share forecast of €5.54. They've stuck with a multiple of 9x to reach that new target, which implies about 9% upside from current levels. But there's a caveat: those gains don't come with the kind of excitement traders saw in recent quarters.

Digging into the truck cycle, the team notes that stocks tied to North American Class 8 truck orders typically peak 9 to 11 months after a key uptick in orders. Since we're sitting right at month nine of this cycle, the signs point to a peak close at hand. What really caught their attention was the rollover in the "second derivative of order growth" - a fancy way of saying the acceleration of orders is slowing down, which historically signals the end of the freight equipment buying boom.

It doesn't help that Morgan Stanley forecasts the market's high watermark will involve monthly orders near 50,000 units through year-end, a number expected to be tough to beat given the comparisons. So, while Morgan Stanley still considers Daimler Truck its top Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) pick in the sector, they're clear that the earnings multiple expansion enjoyed in the past year isn't on the table anymore.

On the upside, the firm upped their EPS outlook for 2027 and 2028 by 9% and 16%, respectively, thanks largely to stronger North American volumes and improved profit margins. This margin boost is supported by the recent U.S. Department of Commerce approval for Daimler's additional U.S. content starting November 2025, which should bring cost efficiencies.

Margins for the Trucks North America division are forecast to climb from around 10% in 2026 to 12.5% in 2027, while Mercedes-Benz Trucks posted a slightly underwhelming adjusted return on sales at 6% for Q2 versus expectations of 6.4%. Disruptions in spare-parts supply from Halberstadt's plant ramp-up dragged results down, but a modest improvement is anticipated in 2027.

Elsewhere, Morgan Stanley maintained other ratings for major truckmakers: PACCAR holds steady at equal-weight with an increased target to $125, Volvo stays equal-weight with a price target pushed up to SEK355, and Traton remains underweight although its price target was nudged slightly lower to €36.

Looking at the bigger picture, the forecast for the North American Class 8 market in 2027 is around 325,000 units-up 20% from this year and outpacing consensus expectations, which hovered around 15%. So, while the cycle shows signs of topping out, underlying demand drivers remain solid for now.

The question lingers: will the truck market continue to churn with strong volumes and margins, or is the peak signaling a shift in gear? Time will tell, and the market's reaction to upcoming data will be telling.

data.title: Experian Shares Drop Amid U.S. Regulatory Pressure on Credit Reporting Practices
data.description:
The stock of Experian slid about 3% to 2854 pence following a public callout from Bill Pulte, director of the U.S. Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA). Pulte targeted Experian alongside its industry peers Equifax and TransUnion for allegedly inflating costs for American consumers seeking credit reports.

Highlighting the issue of rising credit report prices, the FHFA boss revealed that the agency is actively mulling a substantial overhaul of the current tri-merge credit reporting system. Specifically, the FHFA is seriously considering cutting the required credit bureaus involved in mortgage lending decisions from three to two, a shift that could reshape market dynamics significantly.

Given that Experian derives a notable chunk of its business-to-business revenue from U.S. mortgage credit data, these regulatory developments raise concerns about future income streams. Industry voices, including the Mortgage Bankers Association, had previously flagged lenders' pain points, reporting 40-50% hikes in credit report fees, lending credibility to the FHFA's heightened scrutiny.

The collective naming of Experian, Equifax, and TransUnion by the regulator effectively injected a wave of sector-wide caution, as investors reassessed the regulatory risk cloud looming over these firms. This backdrop amplified selling pressure on Experian's shares in particular, which moved sharply lower in otherwise modest market conditions.

On the same day, the broader UK market saw a contained dip, with the FTSE 100 index only slightly off amid anticipation of U.S. payroll data and ongoing concerns around interest rate trajectories. Meanwhile, rising gilt yields and elevated oil prices added some cautious tension, but none matched the concentrated hit experienced by Experian's stock.

The bearish move carries extra significance when placed against Experian's stock performance over the past year, as the share price had previously reached a peak near 3987 pence. The current retreat highlights how sensitive Experian's valuation is to shifts in U.S. regulatory policy, underscoring the pivotal role the American market plays in its overall business.

Today's tumble, dragged down by regulatory headwinds and the potential for altered credit reporting requirements, underscores an evolving threat to industry status quo. For the big three credit bureaus, navigating this will be critical as the U.S. government signals a strong intent to tame costs passed on to consumers.

With mortgage lenders reportedly feeling the pinch of elevated credit report prices, could regulatory intervention be just the start of more significant reforms? The credit reporting business, a cornerstone of modern lending, might be due for a shakeup that could reshape how player profitability is structured.
